status_reason: Material, quantity and location are known, so a provisional first assessment is possible; the reuse premise and the Raman premise are both rejected, and the new calibration depends on blend data not yet available.
answer: The old NIR calibration cannot be assumed valid for the new API and excipient blend; it must be re-tested and most likely replaced by a new calibration. Adding Raman does not keep it valid either, because a combined NIR+Raman model is a new model that needs its own calibration and validation. First test NIR on the new blend at the feed frame against independent laboratory reference values, with Raman as a comparison arm.

inline.headline: Test NIR diffuse reflection at the feed frame on the new blend, with the old calibration as baseline
inline.probe: NIR diffuse reflection probe for powder
inline.install: tablet press feed frame, at the same spot as any second probe
inline.fiber: silica Vis-NIR, 350-2400 nm (covers NIR up to 2400 nm; the 2400-2500 nm end of the NIR range is outside this fiber family)
inline.test_against: Raman probe with 785 nm excitation at the same spot (Raman shift in cm-1)
inline.not_final_because: The published feed-frame study supports testing NIR with Raman but does not prove this blend; the old calibration must be re-tested and likely replaced, and reference values must come from independent laboratory analysis.

problems.text: The existing calibration cannot be assumed valid for the new formulation: NIR calibrations are chemometric models built and validated for a specific matrix, so the old model must be re-tested and most likely replaced.

Adding Raman does not keep the old calibration valid: Raman adds complementary information, and a combined NIR+Raman model is built on newly fused data, which needs its own calibration and validation on the new blend.
NIR bands are broad and overlapping, so the new API and excipients can change the spectra; check this on lab spectra of the new blend before relying on any model.
Raman signals are weak and can be masked by fluorescence from organic compounds; check the Raman spectra of the new blend for a fluorescence background before committing to Raman.

methods.why: It is the existing pilot method, is suited to online use with remote fiber probes, and penetrates into dense solids; diffuse reflection probes suit powders.
It carries information complementary to NIR; the feed-frame study used a 785 nm Raman probe, with the Raman shift in cm-1 as the axis.
Add only if NIR alone fails on the same validation data; the combination is a hypothesis that must beat the best single method.
Mid-IR absorption limits MIR to very thin layers, and the ATR probe suits liquids, pastes and soft solids rather than a powder in the feed frame.

questions.q: What are the API and excipients of the new blend, and what is the API concentration range?
questions.why: Overlapping NIR bands depend on the chemistry, and the calibration range must cover the new blend.

questions.q: Which reference method will give the API concentration, and what accuracy is required?
questions.why: Validation needs independent reference values and an acceptance limit to judge the models.

questions.q: Can you provide samples of the new blend across the concentration range for laboratory analysis?
questions.why: A new calibration must be built and validated on the new formulation.

questions.q: Can the NIR and Raman probes sample the same spot in the feed frame?
questions.why: Only a combined probe guarantees the same spot; separate probes need synchronised acquisition.

questions.q: Does the new blend fluoresce, or does the current pilot already show a fluorescence background?
questions.why: Fluorescence can mask Raman signals, which decides whether Raman is worth adding.

experiment.objective: Decide whether the old NIR calibration transfers to the new blend and whether adding Raman beats NIR alone.
steps: Prepare samples of the new blend across the API concentration range and obtain independent laboratory reference values.
Apply the existing NIR calibration to the new-blend spectra without refitting and record the prediction error against the reference values.
Build a new NIR model on the new blend and validate it on held-out samples.
Measure the same samples with a 785 nm Raman probe at the same feed-frame spot, and check the spectra for fluorescence.
Compare the NIR-only model with a low-level fused NIR+Raman PLS model on the same validation set; keep Raman only if it wins.
references: De Man, A, et al. (2024). Evaluating the improvement of blend potency measurements in the feed frame of a rotary tablet press using combined NIR and Raman spectroscopy. Analytical Chemistry, 96(26), 10586-10593.
experiment.go_no_go: Acceptance criteria come from the client; none are given in the enquiry, so the client must define the prediction error limit before the trial.

pathway.key_features: Not yet identified; the key NIR and Raman features of the new blend must be found in the laboratory trials.
pathway.path_reason: Key spectral features and a new calibration on the new blend are not yet identified; the AFS pathway starts with a multi-method lab test on the customer process.

multispectral.why: NIR detects hydrogen bonds and asymmetric polar groups, while Raman provides the molecular backbone and symmetrical non-polar groups.
multispectral.test: On the same validation set, the fused NIR+Raman PLS model must beat the best single-method (NIR) model in prediction error; if it does not, drop Raman.

assumptions: The current NIR pilot uses a diffuse reflection probe in the feed frame.
The new API and excipients are powders compatible with the feed frame.
A second probe can be fitted at the feed frame if Raman is tested.
